newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Crude Outlook - Calm seen before prices fall.
newsitem.headline: Asia Crude Outlook - Calm seen before prices fall.

text.p: Crude oil trading in Asia is in for a period of calm next week, but traders said they expect premium levels to be under pressure for next month trading.
Regional grades have mostly been placed for February liftings, while most March liftings of MidEast crude have been traded also.
But early indications signal further losses for prices when trading starts again in earnest in a few weeks' time, market sources said.
Two Japanese traders were offering March trading Minas barrels at ICP +65/+70 cents per barrel, down sharply from levels achieved for February of ICP +$1.10/+$1.20.

Japanese refiners are now toning down operations at their refineries after a largely mild winter period. They are increasingly taking the medium to heavy sweet grades of Indonesia, after a period of lighter grades to maximise middle distillates, but the support is not seen strong enough to support the differential.
However, Minas is trading down from very high levels, traders said, reflected in Pertamina's move to raise January term crude prices $1.02 per barrel to $24.13.
Traders said 150,000 barrels of Indonesia's Belida traded at ICP +70 to +90 cents, down from February deals at +$1.10 to +$1.30, reflecting the slide in premiums.
However, traders said the true market was unlikely to take shape until after nominations for allocations are entered with Pertamina around February 10.
Refineries in Singapore are still maintaining production cuts, hurt by plunging gas oil and fuel oil prices.
Surplus product output from South Korea is likely to weigh on Asian prices and could make refinery cuts in Singapore more of a feature of the Asian refining landscape this year, traders said.

Singapore refiners generally take the brunt of weak margins because it is the region's swing refiner. South Korean refineries said they were unlikely to operate cuts in runs -- partly because of legal problems in doing so -- but also because of a need to maintain market share.
Australian refiners tend to operate as a self-contained market place also.
A March Tapis deal at a premium of quotes +$1.30/+$1.40 has offered fresh support to the beleagured crude, but traders were doubtful the level would hold.
"I am willing to bet that the next Tapis deal will not be anywhere near that level," one senior trader said.

Players had assessed the March market below +$1.00 before news that a producer had sold at up to $1.40 hit the market. The previous deal had been at +$1.75 at the height of crude demand for first half February barrels.

Traders said the outlook for Tapis still remained bearish though. Light sweet crude demand was falling heading into the spring refining period, although firming kerosene prices in Singapore were a supportive factor. Spot kerosene rose $2.40 per barrel last week to end Friday at $30.95.

Middle East grades were likely to be quietly talked next week before starting to trade for April liftings. However, Asian refinery maintenance schedules were likely to pick up soon, especially in Japan and to a lesser extent in South Korea.
Despite falling ADNOC premiums for March -- which slumped on average more than 70 percent -- the ADNOC/Dubai differentials based on ADNOC's January retroactive prices -- only came in a few cents.
Murban was cut to $2.40 from $2.42 and Lower Zakum to $2.44 from $2.47, surprising some traders who had expected a deeper cut.
--Singapore Newsroom (+65 870 3081)
